body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students explain how the environment of the Tigris and Euphrates and the practice of irrigation shaped where and how people lived (D2.Geo.4.6-8).
- Students connect the growth of cities, writing and written law to the broader development of early civilizations (D2.His.1.6-8).
- Students examine the origins and purposes of Hammurabi's laws (D2.Civ.3.6-8).
- Students cite specific evidence from a primary source and determine the central ideas of a secondary reading (RH.6-8.1, RH.6-8.2).
- Students organize evidence into a coherent claim about the past (D2.His.16.6-8).

MATERIALS
- The Land Between the Rivers (student overview and lesson reading)
- Laws from the Reign of Hammurabi (excerpts, adapted)
- A wall map of Southwest Asia showing the Tigris, Euphrates and Persian Gulf
- Optional: modeling clay and craft sticks for a cuneiform demonstration
- A SOAP organizer for sources: Source, Occasion, Audience, Purpose

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Map warm-up: locate the rivers and the Fertile Crescent. Read the overview together. Ask: why would people build cities in a dry land? Begin the lesson, Life Between the Rivers.
Day 2: Finish the lesson. Short demonstration: students press marks into clay to record "5 sheep" and discuss why tracking grain and trade led to writing.
Day 3: Introduce sourcing with the SOAP organizer. Read the Hammurabi excerpts aloud; students begin What Do Hammurabi's Laws Tell Us?, working in pairs on the sourcing and context questions.
Day 4: Students finish their claims individually. Model one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph using law 229 (not one students will need for their own claims).
Day 5: Assessment: Gifts of Mesopotamia. Students write an argument about which development did the most to make large cities possible.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a partially completed SOAP organizer and the sentence starters "This law shows that Babylonians valued ___ because ___." Pre-teach stele, commoner and mina.
- Support: let students who need it work from two laws only (196 and 198) for the claim.
- Stretch: ask students to compare Hammurabi's laws with one modern rule they know and explain what changed in how societies think about fairness.
- Multilingual learners: post the key words with a picture for each (canal, ziggurat, clay tablet); allow a first draft of answers in the home language, then revise in English with a partner; preview the meaning of "if ... then" law structure.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit we are studying ancient Mesopotamia, where some of the world's first cities, writing and written laws began more than 4,000 years ago. Your child will read real laws from the time of King Hammurabi and ask the questions historians ask: who made this, why, and what does it tell us? At dinner, ask your child which law surprised them most, and whether it seems fair today.
title: Teacher guide: Ancient Mesopotamia
